newsitem.title: CHINA: China says 1 mln tonnes diesel smuggled this year.
newsitem.headline: China says 1 mln tonnes diesel smuggled this year.

text.p: About one million tonnes of diesel have been smuggled into China so far this year to take advantage of high state-set domestic prices, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.
Smuggling was rampant this year with one tonne of diesel earning about $50 in profit, the newspaper quoted Zhang Deiyi, chief engineer at China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec), as saying.
The state set price for diesel is $264 per tonne at refineries, the newspaper said.
About 150,000 tonnes of smuggled diesel have been brought in through eastern coastal Zhejiang province alone in the last three months, Zhang said. Other coastal provinces were also seeing smuggling.
Inventories at refineries, especially in the northeastern provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang, were rising, he added.
China had planned to increase production to 48 million tonnes this year from last year's 43 million, with Sinopec responsible for producing 80 percent of that, Zhang was quoted as saying.
China allows foreign-invested firms to import diesel for their own use, but many are selling on the domsetic market for a profit, he added.
The state allows foreign-funded enterprises in the coastal provinces of Guangdong and Fujian to buy at least two million tonnes a year for their own use.
Zhang urged the state to adopt a flexible price formula that would reflect domestic and international supply and demand, covering not only diesel but gasoline and lubricants.

Huge imports by mainly Fujian and Guangdong have upset the domestic market, oil traders said last week, adding that China was was considering limiting diesel imports outside state quotas to try to boost domestic prices.
Senior oil officials were meeting in Beijing to decide whether to limit diesel imports through informal measures to boost domestic prices, said one oil trader.
Declining international prices, huge imports and rising domestic stockpiles have caused China's diesel prices to drop sharply in the first half of 1997, the oil trader said.
However, China was unlikely to cut the ex-refinery price of diesel despite declining domestic and international retail prices, officials said.
Beijing had raised the official ex-refinery price of diesel twice in the fourth quarter of 1996 to try to stimulate domestic output.

Domestic prices of crude oil were likely to rise because the government plans to free domestic crude prices within the next couple of years, allowing state-controlled prices to float at international market levels, the officials said.
